parts.why: A page that points at a moved or deleted page sends an agent to nothing, and a renamed heading breaks every link to its anchor, which a check of file names alone once missed.

exempt.reason: git ignores the folder; each session makes its worktree there, so a fresh clone has none
the worked example names a file the reader creates

parts.why: A page an agent cannot place by kind, or whose opening buries its purpose, is read wrong or not at all; and a page nobody has reviewed in months is trusted as if it were current. It reads every page under docs/ and fails when it reads none, since a gate scoped to one folder once passed while pages elsewhere broke its rule.
The index and the contract send agents to code names; a renamed class must not leave them pointing at nothing.
parts.heading: Search aliases

parts.why: A playbook marked proven stays only while a recorded eval run shows it beating the bare model and two lines, so it cannot change without one. Guidance changed with no real case to run it was once taken as better on no evidence, so every proven page has cases drawn from real tasks.
Staging everything sweeps another session's edits into a commit, as it once did in a checkout two sessions shared; the reminder comes before the commit refuses it.
A commit holds only the files the agent session wrote, so another session's edits stay out of it.

src/orders-service-v1 looks current and is kept read-only for audits; an edit there fixes nothing that runs. A fact like this once sat in a parenthesis and was missed, so the contract states it among its first facts and this hook refuses the edit.

Git keeps the history, hooks, lease and edit ledger under .git, and a git config file sets the aliases, remotes and includes every guard reads; an agent that writes one can turn a guard off or change what a command does.
An agent that could add a repository to the outward-write list could then write to it, so only a person edits the list.
A shell write into a git folder or a git config file, or a git config write to a key the guards read, changes what every later git command and guard does, for every session.
Nothing private reaches this public repository, in a file, a file name, a commit message or an identity.

Every delegated task names its tier and runs at that tier's model and effort, as the orchestration rules require. The rule is one binding and one checked line, since heavier tier machinery once cost more than the evidence for it.

A broken hook on main locks out every session that pulls it, so machinery reaches main only through a pull request, where CI runs on three systems; the branch rule does not bind the owner's direct push.

An agent's pull request was once merged unreviewed, onto a target nobody meant. The branch rule does not bind the owner, and gh pr merge --admin merges past red CI with the owner's sign-in; a squash or rebase merge drops the branch's commits, and the proof anchors pinned to them, from main's history.
A token pushed to a public repository is exposed at once, and a later commit that deletes it leaves it in the history.
A subject in one agreed format lets people and tools read the history; the format is the team's, set here.
An agent that reads a secrets file puts it in its context; a deny entry dropped from either tool's settings is noticed at the commit.
While another live session holds the main working copy, a hard reset, forced checkout, rebase or stash drop by this one erases its uncommitted work, as a reset in a shared checkout once did.
While another live session holds the main working copy, a push from it by this one publishes that session's unfinished commits.
A force push or a deletion of main rewrites the history every clone and proof anchor builds on, and a host's branch rule does not bind every instance or the repository's owner.

Agents write on no repository other people own. Outside the instance's list only gh's reads run, and no agent approves a pull request anywhere, so a stray comment, push or approval cannot reach someone else's project.

A token an agent prints from its shell lands in its context and its transcript; the tools' read denies do not cover the shell, so this hook refuses environment dumps and shell reads of the secrets files.
Two sessions that share one browser profile collide, and the second cannot open a browser; each session gets its own, and the agent tool's own plugin stays off.

The commit check fails only a stale page the commit edits, since gates that blocked commits for drift the commit did not cause were routed around; the rest stay out of sight until a session starts and is told.
A session can start work on a pinned repository that is behind its upstream without knowing, and lag nobody reports only grows.
A pin on a commit the upstream never merged cannot be checked out by anyone else, and no other gate notices.
Two sessions in one working copy commit, reset or switch away each other's work; the first writer keeps the main copy and any other goes to a worktree.
A red CI run on main alerts nobody unless something tells each session, and sessions go on building and pushing onto it.
A session that resumes another's work starts from nothing unless it is shown the note that session left; with two notes pending, only the person knows which one to resume.
Hooks and pages run from the main working copy's files, so a fix merged by another session does nothing until the main copy is brought up to date.
A line number in a durable page goes stale with the next edit to the file it cites; a method, class or heading survives.
A reporting page that opens with background makes its reader read all of it for the verdict.
A decision record is read long after it was written, to learn what was decided, when, by whom and what it gave up; a record changed in place, with no date, no longer says what was decided then.
Some agent tools load path-scoped rules on their own and others do not, and pages once claimed loading that never happened; every session sees the rules for the file it edits.
The index's cross-cutting chains tell an agent every path a kind of change touches; a chain that names a moved path sends it to nothing.
A change that touches one path of a cross-cutting chain usually needs the others too; an agent that edits one is shown the rest before it calls the work done.
An agent can call its work done while the checks it broke still fail; a session that edited files is refused its first stop while the check or the fast tests fail.

GitHub Copilot and opencode read their own instruction files; if one stops naming the contract and the rule pages, sessions in that tool work without them. That a tool loads a file is checked here, not assumed, since pages once claimed loading that never happened.

A rule that claims a check enforces it, when the check is gone, never tested it or runs only where someone turned it on, teaches that rules are optional; enforcement once advertised was opt-in on each machine.

Every byte of the always-loaded layer costs every session, and added text can draw attention from the rest. Stale doctrine and duplicates once built up there, and a plugin once loaded its own doctrine into every session, so the layer and the wrappers' descriptions each have a ceiling.

limits.what: the contract and the agent tools' pointer files

parts.why: A wrapper's description loads into every session, so one that routes to a procedure that cannot run yet, or to a lane draft nobody has run on real work, sends agents to work they cannot finish. Pages once named a command that no wrapper backed, and catalog rows went missing unnoticed, so the check ties each wrapper to its page both ways and to its selection cases.

waiting.why: it runs by hand today, as its page says; its wrapper waits for M4, which builds its dispatch, its completion reading, its findings manifest and its review mark, so that a plain review request is not routed to a procedure whose machinery is missing
the tracker spine needs the tracker provider and the per-team trap tables M8 builds
the git-host spine needs the git-host provider and the per-team trap tables M8 builds

parts.why: Guidance is a program with no compiler: an edit can contradict another page or ask for a step nobody can run, so each change to a guidance page names the review that read it.
The stop rule counts defect classes from the review records, so the index must list every record as it is, and the pages written before the review existed must each have one.

A claim recorded because it was plausible, not because it was checked, is how a confident wrong answer gets merged; a fix record marks each claim in its report verified or inferred, so a reader knows which ones to trust.

A plan nobody can read in one sitting is approved unread: a Key points block over 200 words, or a table cell over 60, buries what the approver must know. Only draft plans are read, since approved ones are frozen.
In an instance made from the kit, a hand edit to a file the kit owns is lost at the next upgrade, or blocks it; it fails here until the kit's copy is back or the instance keeps its own on record.
A page marked proven must hold its evidence, an unproven one must name the milestone that will prove it, and neither mark may move quietly: a proven page marked unproven leaves the eval gate.

retired.why: page_kinds holds the review-date rule now, with the same cases, beside the kind and opening rules (M3 slice A1).
